items.title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01
items.q: Nellie Lutcher was on the piano... Paul Barnes on saxophone... that was in 1932.

ctx.x: The Cajun country is what I meant to say, over that way.

D.D. heard him sing that and D.D. picked it up from him. Yeah. But D.D. didn't get the thing right, you see. Now I'm going to give you an idea how he'd go. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. That's where the Mayor of Pompon added. Yeah. But D.D. got it mixed up. D.D. came out. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. Yeah, he got it wrong and it just spread like that. So, well anyway, we had Nellie Lutcher, that was our piano player, and I can forget her father's name, he was our bass player, and a…

items.title: 68426_Nellie Lutcher oral history interview
items.q: It was called the Southern Rhythm Boys. And in one of these groups I think Paul Barnes, the wonderful Paul Barnes, from New Orleans, was in this group.

ctx.x: When you started writing for big bands at a very early age, was there any particular arranger that you were aware of or any particular band whose arrangements appealed to you that made you want to write?

Well, I can't really say so. I think I liked the idea of writing and had a good sense of harmony and a good sense of doing this type of thing, and being around people that were doing it. These guys were writing all the time, particularly this Al Wilson, and as I mentioned, Paul Barnes. These guys were always writing and it just sort of struck me that this is something that I would enjoy doing, see. And as I say, Mary Lou Williams was of course writing at the same time, but I can't say that -- I really can't say…
think, to really make a name for herself as an arranger.
